The appellant could not rest its case merely on r.18 (a) and say that having acted under that rule there was nothing more to be said and that the industrial court cannot inquire into the causes that led to termination of the service under r 18 (a). The Industrial Tribunal had no power to enquire into the cause that might have led to a termination of services even under a rule like 18(b) and if it is satisfied that the action taken under such a rule was a colourable exercise of power or as a result of victimisation, or unfair Labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to interfere with such termination in the manner indicated above. The fact that the employer did not attempt to do so before it could be said that there was no evidence for it to justify its action must suffer from the vice of victimisation and unfair labour practices which were secured to industrial employees through industrial adjudication for over a long period of time now.

The appellant filed a suit in the Court of Small Causes at Ahmedabad for declaration that he was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the theatre. The Trial Judge passed an order disallowing the objection to the question raised by the respondent. On appeal, the High Court set aside the trial court 's order on the ground that the question was already concluded by the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the agreement dated December 1, 1960 was barred by the principle of res judicata and estoppel under section 92 of the Evidence Act since the question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issue of resjudicata in a revision application filed against an order refusing to uphold an objection to certain question asked to a witness under examination. The true nature of order brought before the High court and the dimensions of the dispute covered thereby apparently got blurred and the High Courts proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Court, and which could not be decided by the High 'Court until the parties had opportunity to lead oral evidence thereon. It was for the trial Court in the first instance to decide that question and there after the High, Court could, if the matter were brought before it by way of appeal or in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, have decided that question over again to the extent to which the court, viz., the trial courts in the instant case, proposed to go into that question. [445 B D] The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court has held in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, ; , that the expression " case" is restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code to the entire proceedings in a civil court. To interpret the expression 'case ' as an entire proceeding only and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved litigant where it is most needed and may resulting in the perpetration of gross injustice. But it was not decided in Major Section section Khanna 's case that every order of the court in the course of a suit amounts to a case decided. A consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the Court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court, the terms of section II of the Civil Procedure Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [441 C D] Major section section Khanna V. Brig. H. J., Dillons, , referred to.

The respondent was appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The State Government issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms and conditions contained in the said order including the period relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms, he was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao ny. On 29th August, 1979 he was declared unfit by a letter dated 31st March, 1982 on the basis of Vigilance Report and no opportunity had been given to him to show cause why such action should not be taken against him. The order was challenged before the High Court contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period for his appointment beyond 30th August 1985 or by giving one month 's notice. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the scheme under which the respond ent had been appointed provided for an appointment by contract for a specified term which can be extended upto 30th of August, 1985 and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he attained 58 years of age. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in disposing of the Writ petition on 24.3.1988 declaring that the respondent was entitled t o salary upto 30.8.1985 when the order of termination of service served on him was found to be an invalid one. It is on this basis that the High court had while setting aside the order by its order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the responden ts were entitled to salary upto the period he was enti tled to remain in service and further observed that it was open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the respondent for continuance in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. [243D E] 1.2 The High Courts while setting the order dated 26th July, 1988 did not make out that the respon dents had put forward at that stage such a case. His only case was that the interim order that had been passed on 10.7.86 entitled him to be re instated in service even though there was no order of extension of service. If the respond al was really aggrieved by the Judgment dated 24. 3.1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that did not do but on the other hand he proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be reinstatement in service notwithstanding the fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th September, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been made by this Court.

The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 I.P.C., on the ground that he had no motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) there was no reason to doubt the testimony of P. Ws. 1 to 3 and that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge; (2) P.W. 3, an old woman of 69 years, stated in her evidence that she did not remember if she had told the Police that the accused made a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased; and (3) P,W. 4, an young lady of 69 year, stated that she saw the accused making a gestures as if she was stabbing her. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1 ) The High court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thou ht that an order of conviction could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial & compelling reasons". However, in some cases, Ramabhupala Reddy & Ors. vs The State of Andhra Pradesh & Anr., ; Bhim Singh Rup Singh vs State of Rajasthan, A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460, Bhim Singh, Rup Singh & Ors., vs State, of Rajasthan A.l. R.

Section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 provides that a public servant who commits the offence of criminal misconduct as defined in section 21 of the Indian Penal Code shall be punishable with imprisonment for not less than two years. Section 6(i)(C) provides that if he or any person on his behalf is in possession or has, at any time during the period of his office, been in possession, for which the public servant cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income, such public servant shall be guilty of an offence under section 5 of the Act. Section 7(1) provides for punishment of imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years and section 6(2)(a) provides an additional mode of proving an offence punishable under section 161 or section 165 of the Penal Code or under sub section (2) or sub section 3A or sub s.(3) of section 5. The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was convicted by the High Court and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 25,000/ in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) Section 6 (1)(C), which is in pari materia with section 5(3) and (5) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act, does not create a new offence but only provides an alternative mode of proof of evidence; (ii) The High Court erred in holding that section 6 (i)(c), which was in appli cation to the case of the High Courts and Supreme Court Judges, did not fall within the purview of the provisions contained in clauses 4 and 5 of Article 124 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1973 is not applicable to a Judge or Chief Justice of a High Court since he cannot be removed from his office unless and order to that effect is passed by the President in accordance with clause (4) of Article 125 of the Consti tution of India. [255B] 1.2 In other words, if the holder of an office who may be a public Servant according to the wide definition of the expression in the Act but whose category for the grant of sanction for prosecution is not envisaged by Section 6, is outside the purview Of the Act, not intended to be covered by the Act [255C D] 1:3. The provisions of clause (e) have to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under Section 6. It is for this reason that clause (c) has to be read as a part of the scheme under which the Public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. The ambit of the enactment is to be determined on the basis of the public office held by the public serv ice, which office is alleged to have been abused during the tenure for committing the offence under Section 5(2) of Act and it is not the fact of continuance in that office or ceasing to hold it which decides the ambit of an enactment. [256C D; 257A B] 1 :4.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste specified in item 40 of Part 13 of the Schedule to the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the validity of the appellant 's election on various grounds. It was contended that Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were not members of the Scheduled Caste specified in items 40 and 40 as they belonged to a smaller caste group within the bigger caste group of Sunri caste. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the appellant belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with Sunri Scheduled Caste. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is well settled that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste, the other must be a caste. It follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunri Caste and those parts of the Purnea District which had been transferred to West Bengal were not to be considered as belonging to a Scheduled Caste or group within that caste, no question of Sahas being a distinct class independent of the Sunri ' caste arises. The Tribunal was therefore in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as they appear to have done. [390 G H] (2) In view of the fact that the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 was promulgated to indicate those castes who were to be consti tuted as Scheduled Caste for the purpose of the Constitution, it could not be held that the expression "excluding Saha" meant excluding a smaller ' caste group called Saha '.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building which belonged to a lady named Durgeshwari Devi. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215 per month. On the question whether the offence arises only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition for the relin quishment by a tenant of his tenancy, HELD : (i) In view of section 19(1)(c) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, an assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenants is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. The words are "the relinquishment of tenancy of any premises by a landlord" occurring in section 108 sub clause (i), of the Trans fer of Property Act. The word "relinquishment" does not occur in the Transfer of Property act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing. [422 D E] (ii) In the present case, there was no abandonment in the sense that the tenant disappeared from the scene altogether saying nothing and making no arrange ments about his interest and possession under the lease. As the statute creates an offence and imposes a penalty of fine and imprisonment, the words of the section must be strictly construed in favour o f the subject.

The Industrial Tribunal by its award dated 20th December, 1978 held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal took note of the fact that besides the staff of workmen represented by the Union there were several other employees who would also have to be paid dearness allowance at 10% of the basic wage subject to a minimum of Rs. 150/ in the category of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in case of other categories. On the same date, the Tribunal disposed of the applications filed by the workmen under Rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957 seeking a modification of the existing structure of dearness allowance with flat increases in each category. In view of the increase that was being allowed in the basic pay scale of different categories, the award was made on the basis that the overall financial load according to paragraph 33 of the award would be to the tune of about Rs.150/ and that a burden statement was called for from the company and the same was submitted (vide para 23 of the Award). On behalf of the workmen it was contended that having regard to the financial capacity of the appellant, the tribunal erred in making the wage scales retrospective and in any event in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January, 1976. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different mode and it is not possible to interfere with the award of the Tribunal. [177F] 1.2 In the instant case, the Industrial Tribunal on a consideration of the material placed before it came to the conclusion that the company was in an undoubted position to bear its additional financial liability. The question is to what extent the relief should be given to the employees ?" [176G H; 177A B] 1:3. In the present case, dearness allowance linked to cost of living index is ordinarily the best and the most scientific method of computing dearness allowance would yield but a very small and almost a token increase in the size of the pay packet whereas the junior employees would get a large benefit. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they surely would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them That was why the Tribunal thought that an all round flat increase of Rs 150/ to each workman in addition to the benefits conferred by the revised pay scale and other awarded reliefs. [176E F] 1 :4. The award of Industrial Tribunal is made on a basis that it modifies the original award dated December 20, 1978 and the corrigendum made consequent thereto is also quashed.

Section 2(vi) of the , provides that wages means all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would, if the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable. Section 2(iv) defines wages to mean all remuneration, capable of having been expressed in term of money; and section 2(v) provides that any remuneration payable under any award or settlement between the parties or order of a Court, would be included in the main definition in section 2 (vi). The appellant contended before the High Court that section 15 of the Act was applicable to the case because the wages prescribed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed under section 2. The High Court rejected this contention and held that section 2 of the Payment of Wages Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the Award did amount to wages as defined by section 2.(vi). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that before it is held that the wages specified in the award do not fall under the definition prescribed by section2(vi), it must be shown that they constitute part of the terms Of the contract and since an award made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day, and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appel lant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by that award. HELD: (i) Section 2 (iv) does not take in wages prescribed as defined in section2 (vi) and it is difficult to accede to the argument that the rates prescribed by an award could not fall outside the definition contained in section 22(vi). That being so, the basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section 3(vi)(a) does take in the wages fixed under the award cannot be said to amount to a contract of employ ment, the wage structures prescribed by it cannot fail within the term "wages" prescribed by s 2 (vii) of Act before it was amended in 1958.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma on the acquittance roll. The prosecution case was that there was an application by the Department for sanction to prosecute the appellant under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Chief Secretary, Home Department sent a communication to the Department asking him to convey sanction of the Government to his prosecution. On receipt of this communication the Department served a notice on the appellant calling upon him to show cause why he should not be prosecuted under s.409 of the Penal Code. The appellant did not reply to this notice and was acquitted by the trial court. In appeal, the High Court held that proof that the thumb impressions in the acquit tice roll were that of the appellant was sufficient. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that (i) the prosecution was bad for want of sanction under section197(1), Cr. P.C., and (ii) there having been an acquittal of the accused by the Trial Court, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. HELD : (i)(a) The question whether sanction is necessary to prosecute a public servant depends upon the facts of each case. If the acts complained of are so integrally connected with the duties attached to them then no sanction would be required. But if there was no necessary connection between them and the performance of those duties, the official status furnishing only the occasion or opportunity for the acts, then no prosecution would be said to be within the scope of his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. Clearly therefore sanction was required under section 198(1)(a), Cr., P. C., before the appellant could be prosecuted. [1309 F G] (b) The fact that the entrustment and/or dominion here were in an official capacity, and it is equally evident that there could in this case be no disposal, lawful or otherwise, save by an act done or purporting to be done in an Official capacity. Therefore, sanction was necessary under section 196(1). [1310 F G; 1311 A] (c) The mere fact that there had been an 'entrustment of money entrusted to his care as a public servants did not necessarily enter into the later act of misappropriation or conversion, which is the act complained of. Therefore sanction was not necessary under s 197(l)(a). [1410 G H; 1411 A B] (d) The absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The conviction should therefore be quashed.

The appellant, a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49 under the Travancore Income tax Act, 1922. The question was whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the loss of Rs. 11,872 was liable to be set off against the business profits made in the erstwhile State of Travancore. Held, that the proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, did not apply to the assessment of the profits or gains arising under any of the heads mentioned in section 6 of the Act as they were exempt from payment of income tax under the provisions of section 4(3) Of the Indian Incometax Act and the chargeability of the total income was laid down in section 24 (1) Of that Act. Held further, that on a proper construction of the proviso, it could not be said that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising in India only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Income tax Acts. That the use of these words does not circumscribe the proviso and taking out as it were, from the main enactment, a portion which, but for the proviso would fall within the main provision. The word " income " is used in connection with the principal matter to which it stands as proviso. It is a fundamental rule of construction that a proviso must be considered with regard to the principal matters to which the proviso clearly says unless the words of the statute are such that that is its necessary effect. In the present case, there were no positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business " and compel the application of the second proviso to the same head, specially keeping in view the object of the main section i.e., section 24 of the Travancore Act.

The appellant company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947, the Government of Maharashtra decided that the age of retirement should be 58 but the company refused to retire its employees on the ground that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had already been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age Of 55 though in certain cases the company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959, however, the company raised a dispute regarding the retirement age of the appellant workmen and claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. The Tribunal found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns at least the tendency in comparable concerns in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement ages at 60, but on a closer examination it came to the conclusion that the trend was to fix retirement age at 60 and therefore the age was fixed at 60. On appeal by special leave: Held, (i) that there is no indication at all as to how long ago the age should be fixed at 55 or at 58; (ii)that in spite of the infirmities in accepting the company 's case on this point, the Tribunal has taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it has ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; , followed.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1961 and its incorporation in the year 1961. The Board of Directors of the respondent company passed a resolution on May 19, 1965 to sell its assets to M/s. Mitchell Ltd., who had been appointed as inspectors for investigating the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd. On June 4, 1965 the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated May 19. 1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(b) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the resolution passed by the Board on May 30, 1965 was not invalid because it was made by the Chairman of the Board and not by the board; and (2) the provisions of section 237 (b) were void as offending articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution. HELD: (i) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 is merely administrative, it is difficult to appreciate how the allocation of business of the company relating to the exercise of such power can be anything other than a matter of procedure. For sub section (6) of section 10E it was incumbent upon the Board to make an investigation and report that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of M/S Mitchel Chemicals Ltd., was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members and other persons or that the management was guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. The power is conferred on a Central Government but under the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1963, a Board of Company Law Adminis tration consisting of a Chairman and a member has been set up.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on their behalf that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : (i) If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence and the shortness of time, the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determine whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime is made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is too large, the presumption should draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence showing the complicity of the persons in the crime. There is then no question of presumption. The fact that the offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons or more. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the theft goods were found in their houses. It is difficult to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

Section 5 of the , provides that no substance specified as a poison in a rule or noti fication issued under the Act shall be deemed to be a poison for the purpose of the Act. Section 6(1) provides that any substance specified in sub section (2) shall not come within the purview of Rule 2 and there are some correspondence in this regard, when the competent authority held that the substance manufactured by the petitioners would come within Rule 2(x)(2). The petitioners filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the vires of Section 5 of Act. It was contended on their behalf that since the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory appli cation as it is left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance as poison is not automatically made applicable to other States. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223D] 2.1 It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This posi tion is well settled and it would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. It is also not necessary that the same substance should be declared as poison for tho entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance, as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu lute the possession and sale in that locality. No question of discrimination can arise in such circum stances. [222C D] 2:2 It is not necessary for this Court to consider whether there has any power to regulate the posses sion for sale and the sale of the specified poison. It has become a notorious fact, which we can even take judicial notice of, that the substances known as 'thinner ' as it was or mixing with some other substances are taken as intoxicating spirits endangering the life. In many cases deaths have also occurred due to drinking such substance. If the resultant effect of administering into the system provi sions a violent, morbid or fatal changes or which destroys living tissues, the substance can be safely called poison.

The appellant, a firm registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, carried on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53. The appellant claimed allowance of Rs. 2,68,385/ as bad debt written off as irrecoverable by the Income tax Officer. The Income tax officer disallowed the claim holding that the debt did not arise in the course of money lending business of the assessee. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner agreed with the Income Tax Officer and held that the debts were mere accommodations which could have no bearing to the regular business carried on by the assessee, but no interest was charged by the appellant in respect of the dues at the foot of the account at the end of Samvat year. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the debt in question was not one incurred in the ordinary course of business of a money lending, and therefore, the income or any part thereof was in respect Of the other business of his assessee; and (2) even if it was an "accommodation" account to enable the Bombay firm to tide over the "financial crisis" threatening it in Samvat Year 2007, it could not be said that the evidence on record showed that the monies sent by the assesses to the Bombay Firm were not loans made in the normal course of its business. HELD : (1)(a) The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that a debt of Rs 2, 68,385 was not a bad and doubtful debt in the assessee 's money lending concern or any other purpose as preferred to para 7 above. [419 D] (b) It is true that the Tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar, has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot be denied that the findings reached by the tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by evidence on the record. The tribunal has found that the moneys sent by assessee were not loan made in its ordinary course and in respect thereof the manner in which the partner of the appel lant firm tried to explain the position in March 1954 and the stand of the firm itself at all earlier stages support the case of the Department. [420 G H] (c) The Tribunal has found on evidence that the money sent by it was not loans, made in a ordinary course, of its money lending and therefore the income of the asses see was not liable to be taxed under section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. Under Section 11 A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, where the acquisitions otherwise than by agreement, it will be regulated by the provisions as far they are applicable, of the land Acquisition Act. Section 11A provides that the Collector must make his award within two years from the date of the publication of the declaration and that if no award is made within that period, the entire proceedings for acqui sition of the lands shall lapse. The petitioners challenged the acquisition on the ground that as the awards in these cases had not been made within two year of the notification making the declaration under Section 4 of the Act, the whole acquisition proceedings had lapsed. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Petitions. [565E] 1.2 There is no reference in the Special Leave Petition to any to the stay order and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. [567F G] 1:3 In the instant case, the petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the said lands in Special Leave petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the orders of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984, with which we are not directly concerned here. Whatever the ultimate effect of the order was highly important and there is no refer ence in the special leave petitions.

The appellant bank filed applications under section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 praying for determination and computation of the benefit to which they were entitled under the Desai award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant bank under para. 5 of the Sastry Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal in appeal. The appellant bank claimed that under cl. (ii) of para. (iv) the adjustment basic pay was to be as on January 1, 1959 and that this being the maximum permissible under el. (iii), it was entitled to increments as provided in sub cls. (a), (b) and (c) of cl. 5. The Labour Appellate Tribu nal upheld the contention of the appellant and fixed the pay of the workmen at Rs. 2,000 per month for each completed three years of service in the same cadre as on 1st January, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the bank that (i) the words "subject to rules (i), (ii), (iii) and sub cls.(iv) and(v) of el. 5 were wide enough to include the expression " subject to rules" in cl. 4(a). HELD : (i)(a) The adjustment basic wage under para (iv), has to be worked out as on February 1, 1962, the two increments provided by sub cls., (ii and (iii). [905 D] (b)(i) There is nothing in cl.(ii) which provides for a period after the date up to which el. 3(a) works.

The appellant, a hundred star hotel owner, was interested in a property known as the Hastings House Property and that the Taj Group of Hotels who considered it necessary to negotiate with them in regard to the construction of a Five Star Hotel, filed a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding (i) that the facilities available in the Begumbari land would be left unprovided for if the land was given to the Taj group; and (ii) that if the hospital and the burial ground were to be shifted to other land of the same extent within a reasonable distance from the Zoo, it would result in an unhealthy atmosphere for the animals and the zoo would detract from the manufac ture. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i ) the facilities provided by the Zoological Park were totally ignored and irrelevant considerations had been taken into account; (ii)(a) that there was no need to mention the needs and interests of the Zoor; (b) that as a consequence of the letter dated June 29, 1981 addressed to the Secretary, Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services Department, it could not be divested by an execu tive fiat. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1(a) The provisions of the Bengal Public Parks Act, 1904 vested the Zurich Hotel in the Managing Committee of Zoo. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances of the case, it is found that the Government had made available to the Court all the relevant documents so as to satisfy the court about the propriety of its action. [260F G] (b). The High Courts were right in holding that the decision taken by the Cabinet on February 12, 1981 was neither unreasonable nor arbitrary and that taking away of four acres of land from Zoo was not detrimental to public interest. [261C D] (c) It is clear from the records that the State Government had not acted with probity in not inviting tenders or in not holding a public auction but inviting tenders only from the limited class of persons interested in utilising the land for the purpose for which the land is proposed to be transferred. [262D E] (d) The High court was right in proceeding on the basis that the land which was undoubt edly Government land, to start with, was given by the Government in 1880.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had a cash balance of Rs.4,299 on 1st January 1957 and it did not have any overdraft facilities with any bank. The Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58 under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum of Rs,50,000 was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. The High Court in reference confirmed the order of the Tribunal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no valid gift and trust in respect of the said amount as there was a valid gift even though the debtor company was not carrying on any banking business and had no cash in hand for the amount in question on that date. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. The order and judgment of the High Court are set aside and the case remitted to the Tribunal for a decision afresh. [130D] Gopal Raj Swarup vs Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., ; Commissioner of Gift Tax, West Bengal 111, referred to. In view of the decision of the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court, there was nothing in the acts or conduct of the respondent to show that he intended to create a trust or to constitute himself a trus tee. The entries in the books of account could not effectuate gifts.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service consists of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. The power to appoint District Judges is included in the cadre of superior judicial service. Under article 235(b) of the Constitution, the High Court is made the sole custodian of the control over the district courts vested with the High Courts under article 235 as the control given to the High court over the District Courts under that Article includes control over all subordinate courts. The High Court has power to make rules for the posting and promotion of judicial officers. The cadre of the superior judicial services consists of not only the posts of district and sessions judges and addi tional district and Sessions Judges but also officers holding other posts. One of the officers included there is the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, who was posted as a superintendent and legal remembrancer. On March 6, 1967, the Governor promulgated the Orissa Superior judicial Service Rules 1963 which provided for judicial officers working in special posts whether cadre or non cadre, outside their regular line, should be recalled to the regular line after the completion of three years. In exercise of this power, the Chief Secretary to the Government of Orissa, the Home Secretary to Government of India, the Secretary to Govt. of Orissa and the District Magistrate, Ganjam Boudh, were posted as Additional District and Sessions Judge, Berhampur. On October 10, 1966, a special Bench of the High COurt took a policy decision that as a general rule, judicial officers should be allowed to acquire vested interest in the secretariat. In pursuance of this decision, the State Government issued an order on March 6 1967, directing that all the law Secretaries working in the Secretariat shall continue in that post for an unduly long period and the service will not suffer by being deprived of the services of senior and experienced officers in manning the posts in the regular judicial branch.

Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 provides that persons in whom right of pre emption vests in respect of sales of agricultural land and village immovable property shall vest (a) where the sale is by a female of land or property to which she has succeeded through her husband or brother 's son or daughter 's sons of the vendor or vendors; (b) where such sale is of a share out of joint land or is not made by all the co sharers jointly, only the other co sharer and the tenants can exercise the right of preemption in respect thereof. Section 15(2)(a)(i) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 15(l)(b), where the alienation is of immovable property, it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. The right of Pre emptor to pre empt was upheld by this Court in Atam Prakash vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1) (f) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit land belonged to more than one co shar er and had not been sold jointly by all co sharists jointly, the remaining part of section 15 (1)(b) with which we are concerned should be deemed as a residuary clause to ensure that no co share is left out or omitted and not to deny the right to kinstolk cosharers covered by the preceding clauses. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The purport of Atam Parkash 's case was to deny a right of the pre empted tenant to those relative or relatives of the vendee or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section15(1), even if they happen to be co shari ners. The expression 'other co sharener ' was used in the fourth clause of section, and with a view to covering all the remaining co sharen ties not specifically mentioned the preceding two clauses it used the expression 'any sharer ' in the first three clause which was meant to serve as a specific clause to ensuring that no other co co sharee was left out.

A petition of compromise in respect of the entire subject matter of litigation has been filed in this Court. In view of such a statement in the compromise deed signed by the parties and his two sons, the alienees have made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there was no acceptable evidence. The alienees had admittedly been brought on record under order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in this case. In fact, if the compromise is valid and binding the alienor respondent No. 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the said compromise that on receipt of Rs. 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in favour of the alienee in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. When the matter was listed before the Court for recording of the compromise, Sudarshan Gupta, second respondent herein maintained that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The High Court held that once the court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the court to act otherwise. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. It is not in dispute that the alienors had no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In the instant case, there was the allegation of payment of Rs 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too we had not gone into. The factum of compromise is not disputed. Respondent No.2 and his counsel Mr. Ram Kumar have accepted the fact that the parties have signed the compromise petition which contains terms which they had accepted and all parties have accepted it. In such a situation, the sale deeds are subsequent to 21.8.1987. [541C D] 2. The alienations are for about a purported consideration of Rs 4 lakhs. The sale deeds indicate that a sum of Rs l lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. The alienatedees have admittedly been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years ' old by now. [542D E] Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108, referred to.

The appellant company was granted sick leave with effect from December 14, 1969 and its workmen were not entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness. The company applied for and obtained special leave to appeal as required by section 49 of the , but the same was refused on the ground that it could not be granted retrospective effect from January 1, 1975. The workmen appealed to this Court by special leave against the award of the Industrial Tribunal. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) It is well settled that a workman is prevented from earning his normal wages during the period of his illness and there is no justification for the argument that the rate of benefit at about half his wage under the Act should be considered sufficient so as to deny him the bene fit of sick leave on full emoluments for a period of 7 days when he is certified by a competent medical officer to be ill for that or a longer period. Sickness is a serious misfortune to a workman for it not only prevents him from earning the normal wages but is a drain on his meagre financial resources by way of additional expenditure on food, nursing and visits to the medical centre etc. It has not been disputed before this Court that till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave to its workmen in the region from December 15, 1969. [83G H; 83A B] (2) In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on the full pay on the grounds of sickness and in any event the first three waiting days are not covered. [84G H] (3) The scheme of the benefits admissible under the , cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave.

The appellant was detained by an order of the Government under sub clause (a) of section 3 of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of India and to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government. The grounds were served on him along with the order of detention, but nothing was stated as to which of the grounds could be furnished in public interest. The appellant filed an application before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order contending that no particulars of the ground could be supplied in public interests and that there was non application of mind by the detaining authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the grounds furnished were not vague as they did not contain any particulars as required under article 22(6) of the Constitu tion; (ii) there was no reason for disagreeing with the conclusion arrived at by the High court to the effect that the material was not enough to make out that the detaining author ity was acting otherwise than bona fide. HELD : (i)(a) The grounds cannot be considered to be vague merely because they are vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation under article 23(5). [390 D] (b) There is no substance in the contention that non disclosure of facts made by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means of his affidavit in answer to para 15(g) of his petition, both of which have been set out above. [391 E F] (c) The question as to whether the grounds supplied were vague or not is a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration in deciding whether the ground can be considered as vague. If the appellant had exercised his right under article 19(1)(a), he would have been furnished then the very information which has been supplied in paragraph 12 of the Under secretary 's affidavit in reply to para 14(g). [391 G H] (d) The failure to disclose the facts as well as the ambit of the non disclosure must be clearly communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds are furnished. It is not possible to imply any such obligation under article, 22(5) and (6). In the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. [390 G H; 391 A B] (e) The requirement to furnish particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest, are vested in the detaining authorities not in any other. It follows that both the obligation to furnish the information and to consider the detenue 's request for particulars have been recognised in the case in the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya ; , referred to.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. On April 4, 1958, he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations against him were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer, Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy of the unit. " The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground inter alia that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India: (i) that the contained specific provisions for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45 of the Indian Penal Code, which is as follows : "Every person subject to this Act shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. " HELD : (ii) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 make it clear that there may be a valid rule where under, subject to the other provisions of the Act, the Central Government may remove a person from the service. Rules are framed under section 191 of the . Sub section 2(a) provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned; and if he is a junior commissioned officer or warrant officer who behaves in a manner unbecoming his position and the character expected of him shall, on conviction, be liable to he cashienced or to have such less punishments as are in this section mentioned. For removal from serv ice under section 19 of the read with r.14 of the Defence Rules 1954, a court martial is not necessary. The two sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive. The result is that r 14 of Army Rules 1954 is not ultra vires.

The appellant was assessed to octroi duty under r. 21(b) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayat Taxes and Fees Rules, 1960 on the ground that it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with the provisions of rr. 3 and 4 of the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958. The respondent filed an appeal under section 124(5) of that Act before the Panchayat Samiti. The appellant contended (i) that r. 5 of the Rules was ultra vires the State Legislature; (ii) that the octroi duty had been levied in accordance With law; and (iii) that it could not be imposed without the authority of law. HELD : (i)(a) Rule 3(b). does not require the Panchayat to fix octroi limits, in view of r.3(b), what the Panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions and then finally make the choice as regards two things, i.e., the tax or fee to be imposed and the rate at which it is to be levied. Under r. 3(d) what the panchayat does is only to consider objection and suggestions, and then ultimately makes the choice, as regards both matters, namely, (1) the tax of tax and fee to he levied and (2) the rate. But the learned counsel for the appellant contended that the approval of the Collector on January 14, 1964, relates back to the decision of a Panchayat to levy any tax or fees and not with the assessment or imposition of a tax or any further appeal to the Panchayat Simiti under section 125(5). It is true that the opening sentence makes a reference to an appeal tinder sub section (5) Of section 124, but in the context and setting, the heading of r 5 brings out the scope of the rule. Therefore, r.5 must be read along with r.21 and if so read it would mean that before the octroi leviable can start being levied, r, 21 must be complied with. In other words, rs.3 and 4 must be interpreted as requiring the Panchayat not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules. [222 B D] (b) Rule 5 is dealing only with appeals against levy of any tax and not against assessment or imposing a tax etc., and the period of sixty days of limitation commences from the date of the publication of the notice under r, 4 for all appeals is arbitrary and destructive of the right of appeal. But this interpretation, with respect to r.4, must be held to be correct.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1)(b) of the (XIV Of 1947), and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250. The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could not be said to be pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed by the Conciliation Officer on January 9, 1952. Held, that under section 12(6) of tile , the Conciliation officer was bound to make his report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co. Ltd., ; and Workers of the Industry Colliery Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the industry Colliery Colliery (A.I.R. , referred to. The provisions of section 12 (6) are as follows: " During the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal in respect of an industrial dispute, no employer shall, except with the express permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. . be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b). Colliery Mazdoor Sabha, Asanakulam vs Management Of the Industry Coal Co., Ltd., and Workers ' Union vs Its Workmen, ; , referredto. Case law reviewed. Workers of an industry Colliery, Nagpur vs Management, of the Institution, , distinguished.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was not served with all the documents referred to and/or relied on. He challenged his detention by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. The principles applicable in these types of preventive Detention cases have been discussed in the decisions of Suraj Pal Sahu vs State of Maharasthra & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 with SLP (Crl) No. 1265/86 dt. 25.9.86 and Raj Kumar Singh vs The State of Bihar & Ors. ; , referred to. In the instant case, there were grounds for the passing of the detention order but after that the detenu had surrendered for whatever reasons, therefore, he could not have been put into preventive custody. Therefore, the continued detention of the detenu under the Act is not justified. [910C D] 2. The order of detention though justified when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service of the impugned order was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that after the order is passed and before the actual service of detention, there was no proper consideration of the fact that the petitioner was in custody of that there was any real danger of his release. Nor does it appear that before the service there was consideration of this aspect properly. In these circumstances, therefore. the continued retention of the petitioner under the detention Order could not be justified. It is well settled that the power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated under the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence.

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 provides that where a dealer is at the mercy of the Administrator and is help less against the arbitrary exercise of the power by the Administrator, he shall give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission. Section 28 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is also at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down the provision only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an uncontrolled, uncanalised and arbitrary power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of the enactment and the scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Central Excise Act, 1944 afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under section 28(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. For instance under clause (a) the Administrator was expected to have regard to the number of dealers existing 'in the region ' in which the applicant was intending to carry out business as a dealer but the word 'region ' was no where defined in the Act; similarly clause (b) required the Administrator 'to have regard, inter alia, to the anticipated demand, as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression "anticipating demand" was really not vague or incapable of assessing the power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec. 28(1) of the Wealth Tax Act. [955 H; 956 A B] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise, Poona, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union of India & Ors., , referred to.

The appellants, who were appointed trustees of a temple by respondent No. 1, filed an application before the Magistrate having jurisdiction in the area under section 87 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (Act XIX of 1951) for possession of certain properties belonging to the temple. The appellants contended that they had acquired title by adverse possession within the meaning of article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, and were not holding the same as managers of the trust. They further contended that the suit was barred by limitation under article 134B of the Limitation Act. Held: (i) In view of the decision of the Privy Council in Gnanasambanda 's case it must be held that the possession of the alienees in regard to the properties covered by the sale deed was adverse to the deity on the ground that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment from the date of the alienation. Gnanasekar vs Venkatarayudu, L. R. , referred to. (ii) In the present case the suit had been brought against respondents 1 to 3 who are appointed trustees and their application for possession was barred under article 135 B of Indian Limitation act. The suit had not been brought within the period of limitation prescribed by article 134 C.P.C., 1908, but it was filed on the basis that the alienors had been removed more than 12 years before the institution of the suit. Gannachari vs Gnanadan Das, I.L.R. , approved. (iii) The question as to whether a transfer effected by the manager of a Hindu religious or charitable endowment is void ab initio does not arise for consideration in this case because on the findings recorded by the High Court it was clear that the transfer was made by the Manager not as manager but as an individual and he dealt with the property not on the footing that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowments.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the District Magistrate and the appellate authority under the Jammu & Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989. The writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge who held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsara Theatre by virtue of clauses 13 and 18 of the partnership deed and since it was only the licensee who was held responsible under the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the license and answerable to the licensing authority for all commissions and omissions in the Cinema premises, he could not have any right or interest in the licence which was granted to Ved Gupta in his individual capacity as representing the partnership. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that since the licence had been granted in favour of Ved Gupta by proceedings of his predecessor in interest, he did not have the possession of the premises and he was not entitled to claim a renewal of licence. On appeal by the State Government, the Division Bench reversed the decision of the Single Judge dismissing the writ peti tion. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned order passed by District Magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema show in the theatre without a licence in contravention of the law. [582C D] 2. It is now well settled that all the grounds stated by the Division Benches of the High Courts for upsetting the judgment of the learned Single Judge, dismissing the Writ Petition are incorrect an unsustainable in law. The only other reason stated by them for quashing the impugned order is that the District Magis trate had no power under the , or the Rules to make such an order. This conclusion is again based on untenable assumption that what was done by the district Magistrate under the impugned orders was to suspend the exhibition cinematograph films in the cinema premises and hence it necessarily follows that where the licensed premises including the cinematograph used therein belonged to a partnership and one of the partners obtains a licence, in his separate name, the other partners automatically acquire interest in such licence and that the privilege granted by the licensing authori ty "must necessarily follow the title in such building and the cinematograph". [566D E] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the impugned Order was violative of principles of natural justice in as much as no notice or hearing had been given to the partnership firm before the order was passed. It was also not correct to say that it could be said on the facts and circumstances of the case that the licence was granted for premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the hotel by persons other than licensee. The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by section 6 F of the Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said section are present, the licensing Authority had no jurisdiction to suspend such licence. [593F G] 4. It cannot be contended on behalf of the State that the license was a grant for premises and constitutes an interest attached to the premises. In the absence of any legal right or legitimate expectation being available to the petitioners, there was no obligation on the part of the District magistrate to afford them a hearing before passing the impugned detention order. [592A B] 5. It could not also be said that it was a sole licensee and that he alone was the licensee.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them for the purchase of the stock of raw materials, unsold finished goods, spare parts, cars, trucks and other movables which were in the mills. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and they were called upon to showcause why their lease should be cancelled. The appellants contended that section 12 of the Act applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian. Held, that under section 12 it could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease was held and this result flows according to him from the language of the non obstante clause which is limited to anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, I.L.R. , approved. The operative portion of section 12 which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease granted by himself and not merely by himself, does not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees and cannot prevail as against them and has been inserted ex abundanti cautela. As Arabinda Ghosh vs Mullick A. Irani, ; , applied. The provisions of section 5 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1954, which is retrospective in operation would govern the rights of the parties in the present case. The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing a notice under section 11 of the said Act as it then stood even before the amendment but it was not put forward at any stage prior to the bearing of this appeal and that by itself would be sufficient ground for declining to entertain it which it may be noted is now sought to be raised by a supplemental proceeding under Order 16, rule 4 of the Supreme Court Rules.

The respondent was a minor son of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972 determined the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh and used to study in Punjab and further held that the land in possession of Raghubir Singh was ancestral. The respondent filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate Authority under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The Board of Revenue set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer on March 6, 1973 holding that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 and that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the sub Divisional Officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling areas under the new law i.e. the Act. The appellant filed a revision application before the Board of revenue for Rajasthan, Ajmer, which was dismissed by the Board on the ground that it was not appropriate for the Board to exercise the powers conferred by section 9 of the Land Revenue Act in view of the fact that the Board had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the respondent. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) Section 221 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not subject to the other provisions of that Act. It is clear from the language of section 221 of Act of 1956 that the appellant has power in appropriate cases to interfere with the judicial orders of the courts. Reference may in this connection be made to Parmessar Singh vs Kailaspati AIR 1916 Pat. 292 (F.B.). In the Government of India Act of 1935 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts ', but sub section (2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High Court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [726B C] (2)(a) The power of general superintendence and Control over all Revenue Courts vested in a Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. It was open to the Board, to exercise its powers under section 9, of the land Revenue Act, in view Of the fact, that there is no provision in law and does something illegal it is open to it to interfere and set the matter right. A similar question arose before the Rajasthan High Court in Kana and others vs Board ofRevenue, Rajasthan, AIR 1916 pat.

The expression "newspaper" in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1955 is defined by section 2(b) of the Act as a person whose principal avocation is that of a journalist and who is employed as such, either whole time or part time in or in relation to one or more newspaper establishments and includes an editor, publisher, newsprint or administrative capacity performing, either by the nature of the duties attached to his office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature. The expression "Newspaper ' is defined in section 2 (b) as meaning any paper containing public news or comments on public news and includes such other class of printed periodical work as may, from time to time, be notified in this behalf by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. Section 3(c) empowers the Central Govern ment to constitute a Tribunal for fixing or revising rates of wages in respect of working journalists where the Central Govt. is of opinion that the Board constituted under section 9 has not been able to function effectively. In exercise of its powers under section 12 of the , the Central Gov ernment accepted a part of the recommendations and made another order on 26th December, 1980. The first respondent, All India Reporter Limited, publishes in addition to the law reports referred to in the second paragraph of this judgment several other books commentaries, digests and manuals. The second respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur, calling upon it to implement the orders of the Central government made under section 2A of the . The High Court accepted the plea of the first respondent and declared that the law report published by the Palekar Tribunal in respect to its employees was a newspaper within the meaning of section 2B of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Law reports published by it were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the State Government on the basis of the recommendation of the Patekar Tribunal was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April 1983. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises. On or about 9th February, 1965 a fresh document was executed and it was stated that the licensor had agreed to allow the licensee to use the premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st March, 1975 and that the licensee shall not terminate the said agreement earlier save and except on the ground of breach of any of the terms and conditions written therein. The licensor had entered into an agreement with the appellant to allow him to occupy and use the said premises for a further period of 5 years from Ist September, 1966 till 31th March, 1988. Clause 2 of this agreement provided that if he commits any default of any terms and condition or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy the licensor shall be entitled to terminate the agreement and cancel and revoke the leave and licence granted earlier and shall be liable to pay damages. Clause 3 provided that the license shall not be terminated by the licensor without notice to the licensor calling upon him to show cause why he should not be evicted from the said property. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for possession of the premises before 31st January, 1975. The trial court passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered eviction of the appellant from the premises. The High Court allowed the appeal of the respondent holding that the appellant had failed to prove that he was a sub tenant within the meaning of section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to get the advantage of section15A of Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947, the occupant must be in occupation by permission of the grantor that after the recovery of the permission a suit for possession could have been instituted under section 41 of the said Act. If he was such a licensee, the non obstante clause of Section 15A(1) would give him the status and protection of a tenant in spite of there being anything to the contrary in any other law or in contract. But if he was not a licensee under a subsisting agreement on 1st February, 1973 then he did not get the benefit of the amended provision of the Act. [1065B C] 1.2 In determining whether an agreement creates between the parties the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & others vs Shri Vishwa Nath & 5 others, [1987] 2 Scale 27, held inapplicable.
