Errington vs Erringle, ; , referred to. 1.3 In determining if an agreement created a lease rather than a licence it would be construed not as a mere licence but as a lease. But the character of the transaction turns on the operative intent of the par ties. To put precisely if an interest in immovable property entitling the transferee to enjoyment was created, it was a lease; if permission to use land without exclusive possession was alone granted, a licence was the legal result.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State of Dholpur. He applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni. The permit had been renewed from time to time upto December 2, 1947. On January 26, 1950, the United State of Rajasthan was formed by a Covenant entered into by fourteen Rulers of Rajasthan including those who had formed the Former State of Jaipur. In June 1947, the respondent applied for the grant of a permit under article 295(2) of the Constitution in respect of certain commodities which had been included in the United state of Rajasthan through the Matsya Union. The respondent 's case was that in view of article 295 (2) Of the Constitution he was not bound by any liability which might have arisen against him by virtue of the continuance of the old laws till they were repealed or altered by the new State. Held, that on a true construction of article VI of the Covenant it was clear that the rights arising under the old law in the subjects of the merging States would continue and these subjects would have the same rights against the new States as they would have under the existing laws against the merged State. The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the existing law till they are repealed or changed, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merising State if there was any liability on the merling State. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

Section 3 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933 provides that no person shall, within a notified area, set up, establish or use any place for the purchase or sale of a notified commercial crop except under and in accordance with the conditions of a licence granted to him by the Collector. Under section 4(1) of the Act, the State Government has power to exempt from the operation of the said section any person who carries on the business of purchasing or selling any commercial crop in quantities not exceeding those prescribed by rules made under the Act. Section 5 provides that "no person shall within a specified period apply for exemption from the provisions of this Act in respect of any notified commercial crops which have been grown by him, unless he is registered as a dealer under the Madras Co operative Societies Act, 1932. " The appellants who were dealers in cotton and groundnut, who had failed to take out licences as provided in section 5(1), filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions Of the Act on the ground that they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions contravened article 19(i)(f). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants: (1) that the restrictions imposed by section 5 are not only unreasonable but tend to defeat the very purpose of the legislation; (2) that in view of the entire scheme of the , the impugned provisions of the impugned Act constitute reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to do business and, therefore, they were valid. HELD : (1)(a) The Act is an integrated one and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crops by providing for better regulation of buying and sale of commercial crop. [108 B] (b) There is no substance in the contention that the impugned sections are violative of articles 19 (i)(g) and (g) of Constitution. [109 D] (c) The provisions of section 5 do not offend article 19 (1), (f) & (g). The Act, therefore.

The appellant was convicted for the murder of one Ramchander and sentenced to death under section 302 Indian Penal Code. His appeal to the High Court against his conviction and sentence were dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the conviction must be maintained but (ii) the sentence should not be reduced to transportation for life because of the difference of opinion in the High Courts, not ascribe any particular blow either to Tukaram or to Nilia though he did not want to enter a woman 's name. HELD : (i)(a) It is well settled that a common intention presupposes prior concert and arrangement. In a case like that, each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for an act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted of the murder however clearly an intention to kill could be proved in his case: Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs King Emperor, A.I.R. 1946 P.C. 45 and Mahbub Shah vs King, L. R. 52 I.A. 225, referred to. (b) The High Court was right in holding that the conviction of the appellant under section 326 could not be maintained unless two Judges concur because of section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In the present case there is no evidence of any prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan and as such it cannot be said that the appellants were guilty of the offence of murder. [1090 F G] (ii)(a). There was nothing to show that there was previous meeting of mind to form the pre arranged arrangement, or even if it be accepted that this evidence is indicative of prior concert.

The petitioner was appointed as a Section Officer under the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules, which provided that if he was in Class I or Class II service or post, he would be retired compulsorily by exercising the power under Rule 57(j) after he has attained the age of 50 years; and in other cases after he had attained the normal age of 55 years. The petitioner challenged the order of compulsory retirement on the ground that the impugned order was contrary to the judgment delivered by this Court in Tahilia ni 's case. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 56 (j) is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis, i.e., in a class I or class II service. A person can be in Class II or Class III service or a post even when he holds a post of either class substantively or temporarily or on officiating basis. Instances are abundant where officers are promoted to Class I and Class II Service or post on substantive basis and such officiation lasts for a number of years. officiating promotion certainly does not confer a right to the post and at any time the Government servant may be sent back to his substantive post. There is, however, no reason why sub clause (i) should be confined to service or posts held on substantive appointment. [638C D] 2. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) has a purpose behind it.

The deceased was the husband of respondent No. 1 and father of respondents Nos. 2 to 5. The deceased died intestate on 12.1.1961. Respondent No. I filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on the ground that the medical examination report showed that there was a concluded contract between the deceased and the Life Insurance Corporation of India. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there had been no concluded contract. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the proposal for insurance was not accepted and as such there was no concluded insurance contract between respondent No 1 and the Corporation; (2) in view of the decision of this Court in Life Insurance Corpora tion of India Standing Order, 1960, the risk under the Corporation policy commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the first premium in full or the date when the deceased had died. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this case. When an insurance policy becomes effective is well settled by the authorities but before it can be said that the acceptance must be evidenced by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance, it must be communicated to the offeror. The general rule is that the contract of insurance will be concluded only when the party to whom an offer has been made accepts it unconditionally and communicates his acceptance to the person making the offer. Whether the final acceptance is that of the assured or insurers, however, depends simply on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have progressed. See in this connection the statement of law in Corpus Juris Secundum Vol. XLV page 986 wherein it has been stated as under: "The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some acts or acts con cerned on by parties or by from which, the law raise a presumption that may be inferred from retention of the premium. The mere execution of the contract is not an acceptance and no binding contract arises until the person to whom the offer is made says or does something to signify his acceptance. Mere delay in giving an answer cannot be construed as an acceptance, as prima facie, acceptance must he communicated to a offeror either directly, or by some definite act, such as placing the contract in the mail. The test is not intention alone. When the application so requires, the acceptance should be evidencedby some actor acts agreed upon by the par ties or fromwhich the law raised a presumptionof acceptance.

The plaintiffs applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.V.O Tractors Export, Moscow, the second defendant. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order of the High court amounts to a judgment or a final order within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The expression "final order" in section 205(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. In the present case the controversy between the parties when the complaint in respect of offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P.C. was disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complaint under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was a self contained proceeding and was finally disposed of on the application of M. Syedna Taher Saifuddin Saheb vs The State of Bombay, [1958] S.C R. 1007. There is nothing in that judgment which supports the contention that this Court has departed from the principle of earlier decisions or has suggested a different test for determining the finality of orders. The Court in the present ease expressly approved of the earlier view at p. 736 where after referring to Kuppusami Rao 's case, this Court expressly approved the earlier decision of the Federal Court and held that an order passed by the High Courts in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding and leave the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen is not final within the terms of section 109 I. P.C., or section 205 of the Govern ment of India, Act, 1913, if it amounts to final decision on the rights of the par ties in dispute in the suits or proceeding. If after the order is made, the suit and proceedings still remain to be tried, and the rights in disputes have to be determined, the order was interlocutory.

The appellant, a manufacturer of processed fabric, was selling the said fabrics to the processor. In respect of the civil miscellaneous petition for clarification of this Court 's judgment dated 4th November, 1988, it was made clear by the following illustration: if the value of the grey cloth in the hands of the processor is Rs.20 and the manufacturing profit and expenses for the processing be Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be Rs,30, being the value at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value of raw materials under the Act and excise duty would be charged to the fabric on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at which the appellant would be manufacturing the processed fabrics would include only the price or deemed price at the factory gate for the processed fabric. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The assessable value cannot be said to be the price of grey cloth or fabric plus the value thereof and not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor 's profits who gets the fabrics processed because those would be post manufacturing profits. [345E] 1.2 If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processing for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the manufacturer as to what would be the prices at which they would be sold in market, and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili ties under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at Which he is selling the goods must be the value, of the processed cloth or fabrics plus the values of the job work done plus manufacturing profit, but not any such other subsequent profits or expenses.[345F G] 1:3 In order to explain the position it is made clear that it is also necessary to including the trader 's profit and expense for the process under the aforesaid Act and rules made therein.

Section 33 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961 provides that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1, 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the Amending Act shall continue to service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayat Samiti until they are absorbed in the Government Service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 he was again promoted as Head Clerk. On April 1 1975 he filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana asking that he should be absorbed as a head clerk. The writ petition having been dismissed by the High court, the appellant has come up in appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: (1) In pursuance of the provisions of section 14(4) of the Act, the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The fact that the appellant was promoted on an Ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed by the Loharu Panchayat Samiti prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be consid ered for promotion but, whether the Panchayat Samities have the right under law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post of a Head clerk. He is appointed lawfully to the post as a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [738C D] (2) The appointment of the appellant to the posts of Head Clerk being without the authority of law, he was not entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the date on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June 13. 1973. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Sub Clerk prior to the absorption in government service had been recognised and saved despite the factum that such appointments were made after July 13,1973 when the amending Act came into effect. There was no substance therefore in the contention.

The plaintiff filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that he was the chela of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saana and Sarbarakar of the deity. On appeal, the High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclea and must, therefore, be regarded as property belonging to the math or the temple. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amauli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shiva Shankar Yati and did not form part of the properties of the Math, left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan, deepdan, daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. [663 B C] 2. In the present case, it is difficult to conclude from the material before this Court that the total income from the properties belonging to Math and the deity left any substantial surplus after meeting the expenditure of bhoga arpan was adopted by the Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax. [665 C D] 3. In assessing proceedings under the U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act, 1948, the Amarauli properties constituted the individual property of the Mahant. On his death in 1917, all those properties and wealth devolved on him from his predecessor Shivshanker Yati, who owned three private properties in the district of Banaras. He was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Ghazipur in respect of the two fixed deposits made by him in the Bank of Bengal of Rs. 45,000. He had also inherited the personal properties which were transferred by Mahant Shivasis from time to time and none of those transfers was challenged by the plaintiffs in the present suit. [664 D E] 4.

The appellants, who were displaced persons from West Pakistan, were allotted certain quasi permanent allotments of 24 standard acres and 5 units in the village of Raikot. The allotment was made out of the land released upon the cancellation of the allotment of lands in favour of the appellants under section 16(1) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The appellants applied for review of the order cancelling their allotments on the ground that the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land at all. This application was rejected by the Assistant Custodian on the view that r. 14(6) of 'the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952, stood in the way of cancellation of allotments made in favours of the appel lants under section 17(1). The appellants moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of cancellation. The High Court held that r, 14(5) was not applicable to the case and quashed the orders cancelling the allotment. On appeal by special leave: Held, (i) that r 74 of the Evacuee Property rules which came in force on August 22, 1949, stood repealed on July 23, 1952 and the notification issued thereunder was valid. The power conferred by sub section (1) Of section 19 of the Act is to prevail notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. (ii)that r. 74 does not help the appellants because there is nothing on record to show that a managing officer or managing corporation was appointed with respect to evacuee property acquired under the notification dated March 24, 1955, and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation, of allotment.

The State Public Service Commission issued an advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari. The advertisement was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, a corrigendum was published on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in three stages written, and interview or personality test was not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the written examination were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission cancelled the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of it. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the viva voce, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examination. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. [125B C] 1.2 The State Public Services Com mission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not hav er have suffered; public time would not be wasted in requiring re doing of what had once been done, and the litigation could have be avoided. [126C D] 1:3 In the instant case, when no defect had been pointed out by the High Court, there is no justification to cancel the written parts of the Recruitment Examination. On account of improper feeding into the computa tion some of the candidates who had better performance in the oral examination were also not called for interviewed but were further finally selected, and since upon an enquiry was factually established, the public service Commission decided to cancel it.

The appellant filed a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, the interest which was the subject matter of the suit devolved upon Shiam Das as he was elected to be the Mahant of the said Dera. In appeal by special leave: HELD: (i) The suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the respondent. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, Rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject mater of the Suit and the interest is the interest or for any other reason. Order 22 rule 10 is not confined to devolution of interest of a party by death, it also applies if the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such a case the successor to the head is sued and as it was in the same representative capacity that the appeal was sought to be continued against Shiam Dass, Order 22 Rule 10 would apply. [490 D E] (ii) The word interest which is referred to in this Rule means interest, in the properties i. e., thesubject matter of a suit and the interests is the interests of the person who was the party to the suit.

Rule 2 of the Hyderabad Civil Services Rules provides that every Government employee, not being a workman and not belonging to the last Grade Service shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the age of 60 years. Rule 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh State Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules provides for compulsory retirement of all Government employees except those who would have retired at the age Of 55 years on the evening of the first day of July in which they attained the age fixed by the lastday of the following month. Rule 4(1)(a) provides that a Government employee not being an employee and not holding a workman, but belonging to last Grade service shall retire on the completion of 55 years from the last date of the calendar year in which his attains the are of the age prescribed for 58 years. The appellant who was working as an Assistant Engineer in Andhra Pradesh challenged the validity of Rule 3 (1) (a) on the ground that it had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths who had already attained the maximum age of 55 and, therefore, the impugned rule was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1 ) that the power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitu tion is arbitrary, irrational and unconnected with the object which it seeks to achieve; (2) that the proviso which confers a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they could not be amended retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The proviso to Rule 2 is a valid exercise of legislative power. It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended, as they can be made under the proviso, to Article 311 and that, the power to amend these rules carries with it the power of the Legislature but until that is done, the exercise of the power cannot be challenged as lacking in authority. There will be no order as to costs. [605B C] (ii) The amendment of February 17, 1983 to the Fundamental Rules was made by the Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercise of its powers conferred by proviso to article 309 read along with Article 314 of the Consti tution. It was not a challenge to the power or jurisdiction of the Governor to issue the impugned Ordinance and that his sole attempt was to show that the Ordinance was passed in a hurry as a result of which considerations which are relevant to the fixation of retirement age at 58 were ignored. [505C D] (iii) The power to alter the conditions of superannuation from 58 to 55 is not arbitrary, discriminatory or unconnected with any authority. It can be exercised by the Governor only within one month of the date of his order in which the employee attains the prescribed limits.

The assessee purchased raw materials inside the State of Haryana but paid no tax thereon, in view of section 24(1)(b) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. On these facts, it was held that the sales effected by the appellants were not sales in the course of export outside India within the meaning of section 5(1) of that Act and hence the tax on raw materials imposed under section 9(1). This view was upheld by a Division Bench of the High Court in C.W.P. No. 1227/80. In the appeal to this Court, it had been contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) of sub section (1) are wide enough to include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than by way of sale in the State and use them in the state in the manufacture of any other goods; and (ii) the sales made by the assessees were not inter State sales within the definition of "export" under section 5 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The language of section 9 (1)(a)(i) is plain and unambiguous. It uses the words 'within the meaning ' in sub section 2(c) of section 4 of the C.S.T. Act, 1956. [353B] 1.2 In view of the fact that the exemption claimed for the sales as export sales was denied, the conclusion of the Bombay High Court is correct and must be upheld. [354C D] 1:3 The words "within the definition" in section 2 (c) refer to cases where raw materials were purchased and exported and the word 'export ' was defined in section2(c), as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the State to any place outside it otherwise than, by way o sale in a course of inter state trade or commerce or in the way of export within the territory of India. [355D E] 1 :4. The words 'in the course ' occurring in section 9 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1988 have to be given full meaning; in other words, the exemption under section 8(1), has to be restricted only to export sales falling within the scope of section 3(1); and the exemption is not confined to cases of despatch of goods.

The appellant, a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, was assessed to sales tax on his purchase of castor oil which he later sold for the sum of Rs. 6,47,509 1 6 as mentioned above. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Act on the ground that these sales were not taxable in view of the provisions of article 286 (1)(b). On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1) (b) Of the Constitution. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b)(i) of Bombay Sales tax Act are wide enough to include a registered person instead of the words 'a registered dealer ' and the purchasing dealers have rightly been assessed to purchase Tax under article 19(1)(d) of tile Constitution. Held further, that where the property in the goods passed to the buyer after they had reached the customs frontier the sale has taken place "in the course of the export" out of the territorial waters of India and these territorial limits would include the territorial sea of India. The words " the time of export " in article 286 do not mean that the intention to comply with the requirements of el. 5(2) of article 19 of the Constitution must be taken to have commenced till at least the ship carrying the goods has left the port, though it may in some contexts be more correct to say that it does not commence until the ship had passed beyond the territorial limits of India, or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port.

The respondent wife married the appellant (wife) as a second wife, way back in 1956. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. The trial court held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her mother for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the wife. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 125(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure would apply in the absence of proof that the lady was not living separately by mutual consent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is well settled that an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the Magistrate at the trial level. However, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case on the contrary is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree. Obviously, he has no case of non neglect. His plea is his right to ignore. So the basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. In this generous jurisdiction, a broader perception and appreciation of the facts and their bearing must govern the verdict not chopping little logic or tinkering with burden of proof. [79B C] (2) It cannot annihilate that rate unless it is a reasonable substitute. The legal sanctity of the payment is certified by the fulfilment of the social obligation, not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. No construction which leads to frustration of the statutory project can secure validation if the court is to pay true homage to the Constitution. The only just construction of the section is that Parliament intended divorcees should not derive a double benefit. If the first payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 125 not mathematically but fairly then section 127(3)(b) subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The purpose of the Payment under any customary or personal law must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole scheme of Section 127(1) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning cannot be pedantic but purposeful. The proposition, therefore, is that no husband can claim under section 127 (3)(a) absolution from this obligation under section 126 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or Personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance.

The Collector of the district after perusal of the office note passed order on 25th March, 1988 under which he cancelled the bid of the appellant. This order was challenged by the State Government in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that black listing of the appel lant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing any person in respect to business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an essential principle of the rule of law that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justi fication. It has to be realised that black listed persons have civil consequences for the past transactions under the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation of bid of appellant is concerned, that is not affected. [868C D] 1.2. The order passed by the Collector on 25.3.1988 under which the appellant was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by him was set aside by the High court on the ground that there was no requirement specifically of giving any notice to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant, and an opportunity of making representation. After hearing the appellant the State Govern ment will be at liberty to pass any order in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor.

The appellant landlord filed an eviction petition under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948. The Rent Controller held that the building on the land leased to the respondent was a vacant site and therefore the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation of fair rent in respect of the said premises. On appeal, the appellate authority set aside the order of eviction holding that the Rent Control Court had no jurisdic tion to entertain an application for fixing the fair rent under section 14(2)(vii) of the Act and that therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the rent Controller 's order in respect the premises covered by the lease deed was not maintainable. On a reference made at the instance of the appellant landlord, the High Court held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P1 was only a vacant piece of land and not of the premises which belonged to him, it would be merely one of the issues to be decided by the Rent Authority and would not in any way affect his jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the question of title in view of the decision of this Court in the first set of proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenant that since exhibit P2 was only an order of fixation of a fair rent or eviction, the Rent controller had no Jurisdiction to entertain such an application. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The jurisdiction of the Rent control ler is to determine a fair or standard rent for the premises. It will be anomalous to hold that where an owner files a suit for recovery of arrears of land, it is open to the tenant under the general law to plead that no rent is payable in respect thereof. In order to decide whether the denial of the landlord 's title by the tenant is bona fide or not, it has to satisfy himself that the person seeking eviction or fixation of the fair price is a "landlord" who has prima facie, the right to receive the rents of the property in question. In an application under section 5 of the Madras Buildings (Abolition and Conversion to Ryotwari), Act, 1950, the landlord sought eviction of the tenants on the ground that the order was ultra vires in that no notice to quit had been given as required by law. The trial court held that exhibit P 2 was only one lease of land with no title to the buildings standing on the site in item No. 17(2) and that both parties have all along been proceeding on the footing that the superstructure on item 1 belonged to the lessees. When a petition under article 226 of the Constitution is filed, the Court cannot go into the question as to whether the applicant is a tenant in or landlord of, the building and, therefore, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the LIC on the basis of the open rent fixed by the rent controller. It would not be open to an owner to contend that he should not be asked to pay rent for his own property to some one else. [562 D E; 563 A B] (2) In a proceeding under the Act, whether it be for fixation or not is a matter squarely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of Rent Controller and, consequently, impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil court. But his decision is not final on the issue that opens up his jurisdiction and cannot preclude an owner from contending in a civil court that he must not be required to pay rents for his self property to any one else.[562 E F] (3) It is important to remember that when a petition is filed under article 227 of the Consti tution, it does not provide for a machinery for recovery or enforcement of the amount. The amount has to be recovered by the landlord only by recourse to a civil Court. [563 G H; 564 A B].

The Mysore State Civil Service Integration Rules, 1960 provide for filing of objections only against the preliminary provisional inter state seniority list and do not provide any provision for filing objections or appealing against final Inter State Seniority List as per Annexure 'B '. The petitioner who was a respondent in C.A. No. 1746/67 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the final gradation list on the ground that he had been given ample opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the combined final gradation List dated April 6, 1962 so far as category 6 is concerned was ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the combined seniority list dated April6, 1962 was not final and (2) that a person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity to be heard against the proposed assigned ment of the place. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The combined final revised gradation list dated 4th December, 1973 so faras category 6 was concerned is ultra vires the Constitution. [828F] (b) It is not within the province of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for equation of posts and prepare a common gradation list by integration of services. All that is done is that certain principles are applied in the preparation of the list. These principles are generally found in the rules or executive directions which are known to or are capable of being found out by the persons affected. When a provisional seniority fist is prepared there is a possibility of some mistakes occurring about the facts of a case or in the application of those rules. It would, therefore, be quite fair to give a person affected an opportunity of being heard against such proposed fist before it is finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts may be rectified. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list.[828F G] (c) The principle recognised in Shankariah 's case was confined to the facts and circumstances of that case. [829H; 828A B] 2(a). In the instant case, there is no rule of natural justice having such a paralysing scope. In P.K. Roy & Ors. vs Ram Chand & Ant. ; , it was held by this Court that if a final list is prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the lists is absent, it would still be inviolable and obviously contradictory to hold it to be a final List and yet declare it subject to modifica tion on further objections.

The petitioners are partnership firm carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1991 was in force at the time of importation of the said diamonds under the Import & Exports Policy 1988 91. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to import all other items whether canalised or otherwise in accordance with the relevant rules. The applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that they had failed to diversify their export obligation as a condition for the grant of Additional Licences under the Imports & Exports (Control) Act, 1947 and the Import Policy prevailing at the date of issue of the Additional Licences, and the Export Houses who would be granted Additional licences on or after April 1, 1988 were denied the facilities which had been given to Export Houses, and also from importing items excluded under the import policy prevailing at that time. The said orders were challenged by the petitioners in a writ petition before the Bombay High Court. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the grantees of Additional licences were not only prohibited from importing articles which were excluded under Import & export Policy 1978 79 but also from exporting items excluded thereunder, and further held that there was no basis for classifying such Export Houses into two different categories on the basis of their exports made during the period 1977 78 in accordance therewith. The Letters Patent Appeal filed by the Union of India against the decision of the Division Bench was dismissed by a Division Bench. In the Special Leave Petition to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that sub para (10) of para 218 of the Import and Export Policy 198891 was intended to give an incentive to export Houses to increase the exports in a way as to enhance the net foreign exchange earnings of the country. It was further submitted that there is no difference between the conditions for grant or grant of additional licences under the said clauses (ii) and (iii). Dismissing the Special leave Petition, this Court HELD: 1. The licences issued to the petitioners were valid for a period of twelve months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions. Since the matter has been pending in this Court and the Additional licences issued in favour of the appellants have expired in the meanwhile, it is not necessary that the period of validity of the additional licences should be extended so that the petitioners can avail the same and are able to import the goods which can be so imported under the prevailing Import Policy.

Section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 provides that where any goods are delivered at the time of removal in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer to the assessee, the value of the drums shall be included in the assessable value of such goods. Section 4(5)(d) provides for exclusion of cost of packing which was of durable nature and was returnable by a buyer to a manufacturer on its own cost. The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd. It manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer, falling under Tariff Item 68 of the First Schedule to the Act. The goods were sold in bulk and delivered to customers at the factory in packed conditions and the packing was not returnable. According to the appellant, the process of removal was complete and it is the fully manufactured product which is stored in the storage tankers duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of the appellant that the manufacture of fusel oils is complete and the goods sold in wholesale as well as delivered to the customers at their factory in packing condition and that the containers are not returnable, by the buyers, there fore, the cost of the packing could be included therein in the value for the purpose of assessment of excise duty. It was contended on behalf of the Revenue that since the appellant had effected sales to whole sale dealers only to the extent of 5 to 10% of its production and that 90% of their production were only retail sales would not affect the question of determination of assessable value under section 4(3)(d). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cost of transportation envisaged in section 4 (4) (d)(ii) of Central Excises and Salt Act 1944 for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such packing" incurred by the manufacturer and recovered from the buyer except where the packing is of a durable character and is returnable by him to the manufacturer. The proper interpretation to be placed on the words of section 4 is that every kind of container in which it can be said that the excisable goods are contained would be 'packing ' within the meaning of the Explanation. If this question is answered in the affirmative, then in respect of the goods so sold, the costs of packing would have to be included. [995E F] 1.2 In construing section 4 of the Act, all that has to be seen is whether the goods are supplied in a packed condition. If the manufacturer supplies the drums and charges the customers separately therefore, then, under section 5(d)(1) read with the Expla nation clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods arc sold at the place of removal is to be taken as the assessablevalue, an addition thereto has to he made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Headclerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. On 21.10, 1975, he arranged a trap. As instructed, PW 1 informed him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of Rs. 100. The appellant was charged under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo R.I. for 15 months. On appeal, the High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant is guilty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The conviction under section 165 I. P.C., and section 5.(2) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act are unsustainable. [357B] State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; and Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1, referred to. In the instant case, PW 3, the Principal has averred in unequivocal terms that Ex. P 2 memo had been issued on the basis of the complaint received from the appellant that on getting the explanation from PW 1 he on 18.10 1975 itself passed orders and closed the file. The order made was not disclosed to PW 1 and till 22.101975, the file itself was kept by the appel lant in his personal custody. He had thereafter received the amount of Rs 100 from PW1. This conduct of the appellan t is clearly incon sistent with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW 1.

The petitioner, a public sector undertaking, was in dire need of the flat in question which is situate in a posh area like the Cuffe Parade in Bombay. On humanitarian grounds, he was forced to vacate the flat on the ground that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company 's rules. The Estate officer by his order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner from the flat. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the High Court and obtained ad interim stay of the proceedings before the Estate officer. The High Court allowed the revision petition holding that it was not open to the Estate Officer to buy property in Bombay for this purpose. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provision contained in section 630(1)(b) of the Act is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction and there is no room for intendment. On behalf of respondent No. 1 it was submitted that the provisions contained in sub section (1) of section 630 are a penal provi sion and, therefore, must be read together. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 630(l)(b), makes it an offence if any officer or employee of a company wrongfully obtains possession of any property of the company during the course of his employment, wrongfully withholds it or knowingly applies it to purposes other than those expressed or directed in the articles and authorised by the Act. That would primarily apply to cases where an officer or employees of a Company wrongfully obtains posses sion of any such property during his employment wrongfully withhold ing possession of it after the termination of his employ ment. [176G H; 177A B] 2. The expression 'any such property ' in cl. (a) and (b) are separated by the word 'or ' which must in the context in which it appears be read as 'and ' and so construed, must mean withholding of property wrongfully obtained by an existing officer or an employee of the Company i.e., refers to the whole of cl. [177D E] 3. The words 'any other property ' occurring in cls. (b), (c) & (d) are separa tive and independent of cl.(a) of sub section(1) which makes it clear beneficent construction on the provision in furtherance of the object and purpose of the legislation which would suppress the mischief and advance the remedy. Section 630(l) (b)(i) by clauses (a), (b ) & (c), creates two distinct and separate offences.

The appellant, a public religious trust, was appointed as the owner of the property by the Maharaj who was described in the application as the founder of the Sansthan. The deed provided that the manager of the temple shall continue faithful subjects of the British Government and the said land shall be continued for ever by the British Govern ment as the endowment property of Shri Vithal Rukhamai. After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, an application was made to the Assistant Charity Commissioner, Poona, under protest and without prejudice to the claim made therein that the Sansthan was not a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. The District Judge held that the appellant was a private trust and directed its registration as a public charitable trust. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the order of the District Judge and restored the order passed by the Charity Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) The Sansthan being an ancient Royal grant is a very important piece of evidence to show that though the temple was dedicated for the Darshan by the public, the grant was continued by the Government; and (2) There has been no evidence of any hindrance or restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the Public. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High Court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande that they "cannot prevent people from going to the temple as the temple is meant for a Darshan by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public; (ii) In order to facilitate worship by public, a founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the saints in succession nominated by the reigning saint. (iii) There was no evidence on record of the documentary and oral evidence produced to prove that the endowment was private only because ownership of the donor was transferred to the donee. [523 D E] (iv) The appellant had been given a notice under protest, and without any objection from him, to the effect that he was not an owner as such. The High court was in error in giving full importance to admission of a temple by the appellant.

The appellant was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Marketing and Service Co., at Bombay. He was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 45 and 1951 52 by the Third Income Tax Officer, Cuddapah in respect of his own business of the said business. The appellant contended that section 46(2) Of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, which authorises the Collectors to adopt machinery for recovery of arrears of land revenue was void under article 13 (1) and (2) of the Constitution as the same was repugnant to article 14 of the Constitu tion. Held, that the provisions of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 were not ultra vires article 13(1) Of India, because the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Indian Incometax Act any more than it could be said to be unreasonable. Bhikaji Narayan Dhakras vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , followed. Bhikji Narayan Dhakas vs The Collector of Malabar, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 905, referred to. There is no force in the contention that section 13 of the Act was violative of article 14 Of the Constitution and was void as it contravened articles 14 and 21 of the Consti tution.

The appellants were the employees of the Bombay Port Trust Employees ' Union. The respondents who were its workmen claimed that under a scheme of 12hour shift with 8 hours ' work in a single shift and were liable to be called out at any hour of the day or night. Their claim was rejected by the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that they had not been able to establish that the existing system of work required any modification. The Tribunal held that the strike was not justified because the break up of a 12 hours ' shift into 8 hours was due to the number of actual work hours and that there was no definition of interval either in the Act or the Rules. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on any single day the number or hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13 (3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest. If it is the latter, it is counted as actual work period and the number cannot exceed 9. A working day may extend to 12 hours but the total number of hours of ordinary work must be specified beforehand, and the workman is neither called upon to work nor expected to work; having regard to the nature of the work there is difficulty in giving the intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day. In a 12 hour shift, the nine hours of working day should be so arranged that inclusive of intervals of rest it does not exceed 12 hours on any day and specify the remaining two hours as the interval for rest.

Section 2(1) of the Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 defines 'tenant ' to mean a person who has been in occupation of any building for which the old Act did not apply. Section 40 provides that where any building is constructed substantially out of funds obtained by way of loan or advance from the State Government or the Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a co operative society or a cooperative society or the Uttar Pradesh Cooperative House Building (Regulation) Act 1972, such building shall be deemed to have been completed on the date on which the completion thereof is reported to or otherwise recorded by the local authority having jurisdiction and in the case of any suit for eviction of a tenant from any building to which the new Act did apply, pending on the day on which this Act came into force. Section 39 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (2) no decree for eviction shall be passed except on any of the grounds mentioned in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of subsection (2). Sub section (3) provides that if during the pendency of an appeal or revision arising out of a suit for ejectment of a landlord from any buildings to which a new Act does not apply, the decree shall not be executed except on the ground specified in the proviso to sub section(1), or in clauses(b) A to (g) of sub section 2 of Section 20 and the parties shall be entitled to make necessary amendment in their pleadings and to adduce additional evidence where necessary. Sub section 3 provides that no suit shall be instituted for the eviction of any tenant from a building, notwithstanding the determination of his tenancy by efflux of time or on the expiration of a notice to quit or in any other manner: Provided that nothing in this sub section shall apply to a building during the period of ten years from the date of commencement of this Act. Sub Section (4) provides for a decree for ejectment against a tenant on the grounds specified in clause (a) to sub s.(2) viz. arrears of rent, if at the first hearing of the suit the tenant in default pays all arrears of land revenue or advance tax or advance and interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the landlord 's full cost of the Suit, no decree shall be executed for eviction except on specified grounds. Sub s.(5) provides a bar to an appeal against any order of ejectment passed under sub section 1 or sub section 3 or sub s (3).

The respondent instituted a suit against the appellant for ejectment of three persons on the ground that he was thika tenants under him and the tenancy right therein had been extinguished by section 29 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Act as he was a thika tenant within the meaning of the said Act as it was finally amended by the West Bengal Thika Tenants (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the benefit of section 28 was available only if the decree or order for the recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the 1949 Act but possession of such holding had not been recovered from him; and (ii) even if the suit had been filed before the Act, but was not disposed of by that date, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3. HELD : (i)(a) The provisions of sections 4 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits and appeals, the court hearing the appeal would have to pass a decree for ejectment even if it was found that the person applying was a Thika tenant, the Court before whom the proceedings were pending had to remit the case to the Controller who would deal with it in accordance therewith. [179 D E] (b) The word 'successor in interest ' has not been defined in the Act or in the Ordinance but as words in the statute are under section 2 sub section (6) to have the same meaning as those used in the and the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885, it would, therefore, mean only those persons who inherited from tenants and not those who acquired by purchase. [180 E F] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed.

The State Government appointed a Pay Commission to examine the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. The Committee recommended that the post of Bench Secretaries be upgraded and placed in the pay scale of Rs.500 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. On February 1, 1973, the Pay Commis sioner of the High Court of Allahabad appointed a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers. The State Government accepted the recommendations and issued an order dated July 2, 1976 directing that all Bench Secretaries irrespective of their grades should be given the same pay scale which is given to Superintendents i.e. Rs.200 1,500. This order was challenged by the appellants in a writ petition before the High court. A Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the posts of Bench Secretary Grade I shall be filled up by promotion from amongst permanent Bench Secretaries Grade II and they should have been given the pay scales admissible to Section Officers as recommended. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) that there was no valid reason to give higher pay scale only to ten officers; (ii) that the creation of two Grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Assistants who were doing the same or similar work is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The principle of equal pay for equal work has to be construed in the first place. It cannot be denied that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal payfor equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the constitution. But it follows naturally that equal pays for unequal work will be a negation of that right. And that differentiation so made in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification. To hold otherwise, it would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference.

The appellant company was a Government Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. Respondent 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the demand for property tax made by it on the ground that no tax was leviable on its property since the company was owned wholly by the Government of India and that respondent 1 was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement dated June 24, 1973 entered into with the appellant company. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding (i) that the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 and any subsequent change in those provisions by amendment of the two statutes cannot be availed of by respondent 1; (ii) assuming that section 127A of the Municipalities Act or section 135 of the Municipal Corporation Act which were introduced by an amendment made after the enactment of section 69 (d), could be invoked for levying property tax, there was no reason why, for taxing purposes, the property can be treated as belonging to that Government as distinct from the company which has a juristic personality. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State Legislature loses its competence to pass the Act, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [14H; 15A B] 1.2 It is true that on account of the declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, the legislative field covers the development and regulation of declared industries and not with the ownership of industrial undertakings, it cannot be said that the property taxes provided for in the Act are beyond the legislative competence of the State legislature. [15D E] 1:3 The State Legislature has the competence to enact the impugned law. It is not correct to say that the properties tax provided for under the Act is beyond the competence and function of the Union to regulate and develop the mines as envisaged by the Nationalisation Act. [16G H; 17A B]. Baijnath Kedia vs State of Bihar & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.4 In view of the provisions of article 285(1) of Constitution which provides that nothing contained in any law shall apply to the tax mentioned in clause (a) of sub section (1), the property Tax is not in conflict with the power conferred by the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government to regulate or develop the coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. The paramount purpose behind the declaration under section 2 was that Parliament alone was competent to pass a law on the subject and the State Legis lature had no competence to legislate in respect of such legislation.

Under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 (Madras Act XXVI of 1948), a person can claim compensation only when his right is terminated by the Government under section 20(1). Under that sub section a person could claim compensation for the determination of the rights created before the notified date but after July 1, 1945, for a period exceeding one year would not be enforceable against the Government unless it was established that it was in the public interest that it should be terminated and all rights and obligations arising thereunder on or after the notified day should be avoided under the second proviso to section 20 (1) of the Act. The appellant contended that the termination of his lease by the order dated December 27, 1955, was bad as it did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Abolition Act. Held, that in view of the provisions of the Madras Estate (Abolition & Conversion intoRyotwari)Act, 1948, which provides that a mining lease granted by a private person shall be subject to certain conditions therein specified, the Government could terminate the lease at its option and unconditionally, under proviso (iii) that can be done only if it is in public interest to do so and in such cases compensation will be payable under section20(2). A.M.S.S.,S.C., vs The State of Madras, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 489, referred to. Held further, that the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction, and it was not necessary for the Government to give three month 's notice as required under the third proviso to sub section (1).
